69	                                  Sports with high occurrences of ACLI include team contact sports (i.e., basketball,
70	                            football, hockey) and fixed-object high-impact rotational landing sports (i.e., gymnastics,
71	                            obstacle course races) [9]. In addition to the characteristics of these sports that might lead to
72	                            high-risk mechanisms for ACLI, athletes from these sports often show similar neuromuscu-
73	                            lar characteristics that could make them more at risk of ACLI [10,11]. The most commonly
74	                            reported of these characteristics is a greater imbalance between the strength developed by
75	                            the quadriceps and hamstrings in these athletes compared to athletes from other sports
76	                            or non-athletic populations [10,11]. This imbalance is classically quantified by the func-
77	                            tional hamstring-to-quadriceps ratio, defined as the ratio between hamstring eccentric peak
78	                            torque (Hecc ) and quadriceps concentric peak torque (Qcon ). Other characteristics of these
79	                            athletes that might put them more at risk of ACLI include a low limb symmetry index
80	                            (LSI) [10], in particular in sports with very specific roles for each leg (kicking in football,
81	                            lunging in field hockey, for example), and the need for explosive force production and
82	                            quick changes in direction [12].
83	                                  Interestingly, the risk factors described above are also crucial factors to consider for
84	                            RTS after ACLI. Indeed, deficits in the strength developed by the quadriceps and ham-
85	                            strings are commonly reported in athletes, both at RTS and in the years following [13–16].
86	                            The hamstrings’ role as a synergist for the ACL is important in managing anterior tibial
87	                            translation during landing, with maximal strength deficits reported as a risk factor for
88	                            ACLI or re-injury in a number of prospective studies [17,18]. Quadriceps contractions help
89	                            to absorb GRF during performance, in turn attenuating loads on lower extremities, such as
90	                            the ACL during landing [19]. Deficits in quadriceps maximal strength have been associated
91	                            with the incidence of re-injury following ACLI [20]. For both these muscle groups, it is
92	                            commonly accepted that an LSI greater than 90% between operated and non-operated legs
93	                            should be sufficient to reduce the risk of future damage to the surgical graft [20]. Despite
94	                            this stipulation, many athletes still RTS with strength deficits in both muscle groups at RTS
95	                            and in the years following, making appropriate rehabilitation essential [13,15,16].
96	                                  More recently, authors have investigated quadriceps and hamstring force produced
97	                            close to knee extension as risk factors because ACLI seem to occur at these angles [21,22],
98	                            while peak values occur mid-range [23]. Hammond [24] identified that within a cohort of
99	                            previously injured athletes who met initial criteria of LSI > 90% for maximal strength of
100	                            the quadriceps and hamstrings, strength deficiencies were still observed in 72% of them, in
101	                            particular at 10- 40◦ from full extension.
102	                                  As mentioned earlier, the capacity to quickly produce force (rate of force or torque
103	                            development, RFD or RTD) is a strong predictor of ACLI, in particular for the hamstring [24].
104	                            Indeed, most ACLI occurs within 0–61ms of initial contact with the ground [25]. The use of
105	                            RFD, despite its relevance, remains very limited for RTS testing following ACLR [26], yet
106	                            deficits in RFD are commonly seen following ACLR [27,28].
107	                                  To our knowledge, only one study has examined the relationship between strength
108	                            performance and psychological variables following ACLR utilising the anterior cruciate lig-
109	                            ament return to sport after injury (ACL-RSI) questionnaire to quantify patient psychological
110	                            readiness to RTS [29]. This study showed a significant association between ACL-RSI scores
111	                            and hamstring peak torque, but not quadriceps, in a cohort of male athletes at 9 months
112	                            post-surgery [29]. Additional findings from this study were the absence of significant
113	                            differences in peak strength variables between a group with a low ACL-RSI score (<65)
114	                            and a group with a high ACL-RSI score (>85). However, this study only measured peak
115	                            strength, and there are currently no investigations on the association between ACL-RSI
116	                            scores and other strength parameters, such as RFD or angle-specific torque.
117	                                  Therefore, the primary aim of the present study was to investigate the strength and
118	                            power determinants of athletes’ psychological readiness to RTS. A secondary aim was
119	                            to compare strength and power performance of a group deemed psychologically ready
120	                            for a return to PILOS against those deemed not psychologically ready to return to PILOS.
121	                            We hypothesised that the group deemed not psychologically ready for a return to PILOS
122	 Healthcare 2023, 11, 2787                                                                                            3 of 12
123	
124	
125	
126	
127	                            will show significantly lower strength and power values compared to the group deemed
128	                            psychologically ready to return to PILOS.
129	
130	                            2. Materials and Methods
131	                            2.1. Participants
132	                                 Twelve participants, including six males and six females (20.7 ± 2.5 years old;
133	                            174.2 ± 7.5 cm; 70.2 ± 8.5 kg; 18.2 ± 8.3% body fat) volunteered to take part in the study.
134	                            They were recruited from various university teams competing at regional to national levels.
135	                            Inclusion criteria were having a primary ACLR more than 9 months prior to the start of the
136	                            study because most athletes are cleared for RTS support between 6–9-month post-surgery.
137	                            To be included in the study participants should also have already returned to some form of
138	                            sport participation or have been officially cleared to do so by a qualified physiotherapist.
139	                            Exclusion criteria were any current lower limb injury, any history of contralateral ACLI or
140	                            recurrent ipsilateral ACLR, and any mental health condition, such as depression or anxiety,
141	                            that could influence ACLI-RSI scores [30]. Participants gave written informed consent
142	                            and the study was approved by the local university ethics committee (reference number
143	                            191305), in accordance with the principles set in the Helsinki declaration.
144	
145	                            2.2. Procedures
146	                                  The study design was cross-sectional, with participants attending the laboratory on
147	                            one occasion only to perform psychological assessments first, followed by strength testing.
148	                            The same investigator performed all the tests on all participants.
149	                                  Psychological assessment consisted of the ACL-RSI questionnaire. This questionnaire
150	                            was chosen for its very good validity and reliability [31,32]. In addition, its use was
151	                            recommended in the 2015 consensus statement following ACLI [3]. The total score out of
152	                            100 was recorded, and it was also used to separate participants into one group deemed
153	                            not psychologically ready to return to PILOS (cases) and a group deemed psychologically
154	                            ready to return to PILOS (controls). The threshold used for these groups was a total score of
155	                            81.4%, as a previous study reported an association between scores <81.4% and the inability
156	                            for athletes to return to this level [31].
157	                                  Strength testing was undertaken on an isokinetic dynamometer (Biodex system 4;
158	                            Biodex, Shirley, NY, USA). A standardised warm up was implemented prior to the initiation
159	                            of isokinetic testing. This consisted of 8 min on a Monark cycle ergometer (874E; Monark,
160	                            Vanberg, Sweden) at an intensity of 100 W, with three intermittent 6 s maximal effort sprints
161	                            at minutes 6, 7, and 8. This was followed by five body-weight squats and two submaximal
162	                            and three maximal counter-movement jumps [29]. After the warm-up, participants were
163	                            instructed to sit upright on the chair with their hips flexed at 90◦ . Straps were secured
164	                            to immobilise movement at the thighs, hips, and trunk in order to limit the influence
165	                            of extraneous joint and muscle involvement. Straps were secured at the proximal tibias,
166	                            from which participants would initiate/resist movement. Alignment of the lateral femoral
167	                            condyle was made with the axis of the dynamometer level arm, with the proximal lever
168	                            arm secured at the lateral malleolus. Participants were tested on both operated and non-
169	                            operated legs and at two angular velocities, with all of these conditions randomised. The
170	                            range of motion was from 0◦ (full knee extension) to 90◦ of knee flexion, and participants
171	                            were given verbal encouragement to perform the fastest and strongest contraction effort
172	                            throughout the range. The test consisted of concentric contractions of the quadriceps and
173	                            eccentric contraction of the hamstrings at 60◦ ·s−1 (three repetitions) and 180◦ ·s−1 (five
174	                            repetitions). Five repetitions have been recommended in previous studies at 180◦ ·s−1
175	                            because it takes more repetitions to reach peak torque and it also induces less fatigue than
176	                            slower velocities [24]. These velocities are characterised by excellent test–retest reliability
177	                            (intraclass correlation coefficients of 0.95–0.98 [33]. Each condition was preceded by a
178	                            familiarisation set.
179	                                  The following variables were calculated as the average of the two best contractions at
180	                            60◦ ·s−1 and the three best contractions at 180◦ ·s−1 :
181	 Healthcare 2023, 11, 2787                                                                                                     4 of 12
182	
183	
184	
185	
186	                            –    Concentric peak torque of the quadriceps relative to body weight (Qcon, N·m·kg−1 ).
187	                            –    Eccentric peak torque of the hamstrings relative to body weight (Hecc , N·m·kg−1 ).
188	                            –    Peak Hecc :Qcon .
189	                            –    Angle-specific Hecc , Qcon , and Hecc :Qcon at 10◦ (Hecc10 , Qcon10 , Hecc :Qcon10 ), 20◦
190	                                 (Hecc20 , Qcon20 , Hecc :Qcon20 ), 30◦ (Hecc30 , Qcon30 , Hecc :Qcon30 ), and 40◦ (Hecc40 , Qcon40 ,
191	                                 Hecc :Qcon40 ) from full knee extension. These were calculated as averages between
192	                                 0–10◦ , 11–20◦ , 21–30◦ , and 31–40◦ , respectively [34].
193	                            –    Quadriceps and hamstrings RTD in the first 50 ms and the first 100 ms (RTD50 and
194	                                 RTD100, N·m·s−1 ) for Hecc , Qcon , and Hecc /Qcon , calculated as the ratio between the
195	                                 change in torque and the corresponding change in time in the first 50 ms and 100 ms
196	                                 of contraction, respectively. The onset of contraction was defined as a torque value of
197	                                 1% of the peak torque produced during the same contraction [35]. The time windows
198	                                 of 50 ms and 100 ms were chosen as the best compromise between reliability and
199	                                 ecological validity. Indeed, ACL injuries usually occur in the first 50 ms after initial
200	                                 ground contact [36]. However, Mentiplay et al. [37] showed greater reliability of
201	                                 RFD at 100 ms than 50 ms. The same time windows were previously used in similar
202	                                 research [35].
203	                            –    LSI for all parameters: = ([(operated-non-operated)/non-operated] × 100.

206	                                  All data were presented as mean ± standard deviation, with a 95% confidence interval
207	                            (CI). Statistical analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS V.29. The normality of data was
208	                            assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test. A stepwise linear regression was conducted on the
209	                            entire sample to identify if strength data from the operated leg could be determinants
210	                            of the ACL-RSI score. Subsequently, participants were divided into a ready to return to
211	                            PILOS group and not ready to return to PILOS group. A mixed model analysis of variance
212	                            (ANOVA) with repeated measures was performed to assess differences between groups
213	                            (ready vs. not ready to return to PILOS) and angular velocities (60◦ ·s−1 vs. 180◦ ·s−1 )
214	                            on all outcome variables. Effect sizes were calculated as partial eta squared (η2 p ) for the
215	                            ANOVA and interpreted as no effect (0–0.05), minimum effect (0.05–0.26), and strong effect
216	                            (0.26–0.64), while Cohen’s d (d) represented the effect size for post-hoc tests, and were
217	                            interpreted as small (>0.2), medium (>0.5), and large (>0.8), [38]. The p-value was set at
218	                            p < 0.05.
219	
220	                            3. Results
221	                                  We recruited participants from football (n = 4), volleyball (n = 2), netball (n = 2),
222	                            lacrosse (n = 2), tennis (n = 1), and triathlon (n = 1). Seven participants were identified as
223	                            cases with ACL-RSI scores <81.4% and five participants were identified as controls with
224	                            ACL-RSI scores > 81.5. Participant Demographics are summarised in Table 1.
225	                                  The linear regression identified that three variables, namely quadriceps RTD100 at

229	                            time since surgery; and beta = 0.411, t = 3.498 (p = 0.008) for hamstrings RTD50 at 60◦ ·s−1 .

531	                            4. Discussion
532	                                 This study is one of very few observing the relationship between strength and power
533	                            parameters and psychological readiness following ACLR. We measured a range of param-
534	                            eters during concentric contractions of the quadriceps and eccentric contractions of the
535	                            hamstrings, since these antagonist muscles are involved in many sport movements. In
536	                            particular, the hamstrings act as an ACL agonist by eccentrically contracting to decelerate
537	                            the anterior translation of the tibia during powerful quadriceps contractions. The main
538	                            findings are that the RTD of the quadriceps and hamstrings, as well as time since surgery,
539	                            were the main determinants of psychological readiness following ACLR. In addition, com-
540	                            pared to controls, cases showed significantly lower angle-specific Qcon close to extension
541	                            and lower RTD for Qcon , but no difference in peak torque values.
542	                                 We recruited athletes mostly from team contact sports, despite advertising the study
543	                            to all university sports. It is not very surprising due to the high occurrence of ACLI
544	                            reported in these sports [9]. It is well established that athletes from these sports show
545	                            similar neuromuscular characteristics that could make them more at risk of ACLI, such as
546	                            low Hecc :Qcon or high LSI [10,11].
547	                                 A novel finding identified within this study is the extent to which RTD has been
548	                            identified as both a determinant for psychological readiness and as a statistically significant
549	                            difference between groups. This is the first study to examine the relationships between
550	                            muscle RTD scores and psychological readiness, and, therefore, a comparison of results
551	                            cannot be made against previous literature. The prevalence of RFD as a power deficit
552	                            following ACLR, however, is well reported for the injured limb in the short term [27,28] but
553	                            also in the longer term [39]. Deficits in RFD following ACLR could be due to both neural
554	                            and peripheral muscular factors [39,40] and seem to closely reflect athletes’ rehabilitation
555	                            status [39]. Several training modalities can improve RFD; for example, ballistic training
556	                            performed around RTS [41] has shown greater increases in RFD than traditional strength
557	                            and endurance training [42]. Sprint training also increased RFD (+29% in four weeks)
558	                            in a recent study, while strength training did not [43]. With a potential overreliance on
559	                            isolated maximal muscle strength after ACLR within traditional RTS training [41], results
560	                            from this study indicate a greater focus should be given to training methods including a
561	                            speed/power element in the facilitation of a successful RTS. Examples of such exercises
562	                            include jump squats, mountain climbers, plank jacks, and skater hops for quadriceps power
563	                            gain, and hurdle jumps, box jumps, jumping lunges, and resisted sprinting for hamstrings
564	                            power gain. Physiotherapists should also monitor RTD (or RFD) during rehabilitation and
565	                            consider it as an important variable for RTS. To explain the impact of RTD on psychological
566	                            outcomes shown in the present study, the functional role played by the hamstrings and
567	                            quadriceps in providing stability at the knee needs to be considered [44,45]. The ability
568	                            of muscles to generate force within an early critical window (0–100 ms) is essential for
569	                            stabilising the leg, attenuating GRF [19], and aligning landing mechanics within the period
570	                            of time in which ACLI occur [25]. With residual movement impairments during RTS, it
571	                            may be theorised that such neuromuscular deficits will affect the quality of movement
572	                            athletes display [41], which may be negatively perceived by athletes, subsequently altering
573	                            their ACL-RSI scores. These assumptions rely on the biopsychosocial framework, where an
574	                            athlete’s physiological factors have a mediating role in their psychological perceptions [3].
575	                            However, further experimental studies should be conducted to confirm these associations.
576	                                 The role of peak torque as a determinant of ACL-RSI scores was not identified in the
577	                            present study, suggesting that maximal force production might not be as important as
578	                            sport staff (coaches, physiotherapists, and strength and conditioning staff) or researchers
579	                            thought. This is partly in line with the findings of the only study in this area reporting no
580	                            significant relationship between peak Qcon at 60◦ ·s−1 and ACL-RSI scores in athletes nine
581	                            months post-surgery [29]. However, the same authors also showed a small but significant
582	                            correlation (r = 0.14) between peak Hecc at 60◦ ·s−1 and ACL-RSI scores [29], which is in
583	                            contrast with our results. The study of O’Connor et al. [29] also separated participants
584	                            according to their ACL-RSI scores, similar to the present study, and found no significant

590	                            between-group differences in peak Qcon or peak Hecc , in accordance with our results. The
591	                            contrasting results on Hecc between the present study and the study of O’Connor et al. [29]
592	                            could be explained by the different criteria used to separate groups (low (<65) and high
593	                            (>85) ACL-RSI scores for cases and controls in the study by O’Connor et al. [29] compared
594	                            to <81.4% and >81.4% in the present study). Having some individuals from different groups
595	                            but with very close ACL-RSI scores in the present study could have biassed the results
596	                            towards a lack of between-group differences. Other differences between studies are the
597	                            significantly larger sample size in O’Connor [29]’s study (n = 452) and their cut-off at nine
598	                            months post-surgery, compared to the range of longitudinal time frames examined within
599	                            this study. It can be hypothesised that athlete perceptions within O’Connor’s [29] study
600	                            are more of a reflection of their rehabilitation process. In contrast, for our participants who
601	                            have returned to sport and, thus, benefit from greater sporting exposures, ACL-RSI scores
602	                            illustrate the development of psychological barriers for athletes in the pursuit of a return to
603	                            PILOS, which is a novel element of the current study. Finally, our data analysis was based
604	                            on a linear regression, in contrast to correlations in the study of O’Connor et al. [29], which
605	                            may explain the lack of association between some parameters and the ACL-RSI scores.
606	                                  A novel finding of the present study is the significantly lower Qcon40 and Qcon30 in
607	                            cases compared to controls (differences of 21% and 23%, respectively, at these angles). The
608	                            role of the quadriceps at these shallow flexion angles is significant in relation to the number
609	                            of ACLI that occur within them [21]. Previous studies have shown that individuals with
610	                            weaker quadriceps have altered sagittal plane kinematics during landing and subsequently
611	                            incur higher GRF upon a stiff-legged landing [19]. Similar to our comments on RTD, this
612	                            process may result in a perception of instability during sport participation that could be
613	                            reflected in the ACL-RSI scores. During rehabilitation, restoration of joint ROM is targeted
614	                            during the early phases [46], yet little consideration is noted regarding muscular strength,
615	                            specifically functionally important ranges (near full knee extension) in which non-contact
616	                            ACLI occur (Hammond [24]). Our findings on angle-specific torque, together with the
617	                            absence of significant differences between groups in peak torque, highlight the importance
618	                            for physiotherapists to address strength deficits across the full range of motion and consider
619	                            sport-specific mechanics (i.e., movements such as landing or side cutting, where the knee
620	                            might not be very flexed, supporting stipulations made by Hammond [24], who similarly
621	                            reported strength deficits between specific angles, where >90% LSI was achieved during
622	                            peak torque assessments). The importance of the capacity to produce high torque when
623	                            the knee is close to full extension has also been highlighted in a study on fatigue in female
624	                            footballers, showing that Hecc :Qcon was significantly reduced after a simulated match only
625	                            between 0 and 10◦ from full knee extension [34]. This highlights the reduced capacity
626	                            of the hamstring to stabilise the knee joint close to extension in a fatigued state, where
627	                            ACLI occurs, and highlights the importance of addressing residual strength deficits at these
628	                            angles during rehabilitation.
629	                                  The limb symmetry index has been cited as a risk factor for lower limb injuries in
630	                            previous literature [47], although there are contrasting results in the literature [48]. Our
631	                            findings did not identify it as a major determinant of psychological readiness to RTS,
632	                            suggesting that it might not be sensitive enough to affect athletes’ perceptions during
633	                            exercise. However, we found that LSI for RTD100 in the quadriceps at both testing velocities
634	                            was greater in cases than controls. This highlights one more time that power rather than
635	                            strength could be an important factor that could play a role in athletes’ decisions to RTS.
636	                                  The main limitations of the present study are the lack of control over our participants’
637	                            rehabilitation and subsequent sport experience. Indeed, we could not capture the exercise
638	                            types, volume, and frequency of rehabilitation sessions or past/current sport participation
639	                            due to the long time lapse between the start of rehabilitation and testing for some of our
640	                            participants. In addition, we chose to focus on psychological parameters as our main
641	                            outcome and explore the role of strength and power variables as potential determinants
642	                            of this. However, an argument can be made that constructs such as fear and confidence
643	                            may instead impact physiological parameters through the avoidance of high-intensity

650	                                   small, in particular in comparison with the study by O’Connor et al. [29], which could
651	                                   limit the interpretation of our findings; however, this is counteracted by the fact that we
652	                                   observed relatively large effect sizes. We also recruited athletes from specific sports, which
653	                                   might limit the application of our findings to other sports. The main strengths of our
654	                                   study are the wide and novel range of outcome variables considered (in particular, RTD
655	                                   and angle-specific torque data) and the controlled laboratory conditions in which data
656	                                   was collected.

658	                                   5. Conclusions
659	                                         In conclusion, our findings showed that one of the main determinants of psychological
660	                                   readiness to RTS following ACLR was the RTD of the quadriceps and hamstrings. In
661	                                   addition, compared to controls, cases showed significantly lower angle-specific quadriceps
662	                                   torque close to extension and lower quadriceps RTD, but no difference in peak torque values.
663	                                   The importance of muscular strength across all angles of function was also identified, with
664	                                   quadriceps strength of particular importance at angles of functional relevance between 20◦
665	                                   and 40◦ from full extension. These findings highlight the importance for physiotherapists
666	                                   to address muscular deficits across their full range (by choosing some exercises with the
667	                                   knee joint positioned near full extension) and develop power and explosiveness in addition
668	                                   to strength in rehabilitation. Future studies with larger sample sizes are needed to further
669	                                   investigate the relationship between strength and power and psychological factors playing
670	                                   a role in RTS.

                                  Sports with high occurrences of ACLI include team contact sports (i.e., basketball,
                            football, hockey) and fixed-object high-impact rotational landing sports (i.e., gymnastics,
                            obstacle course races) [9]. In addition to the characteristics of these sports that might lead to
                            high-risk mechanisms for ACLI, athletes from these sports often show similar neuromuscu-
                            lar characteristics that could make them more at risk of ACLI [10,11]. The most commonly
                            reported of these characteristics is a greater imbalance between the strength developed by
                            the quadriceps and hamstrings in these athletes compared to athletes from other sports
                            or non-athletic populations [10,11]. This imbalance is classically quantified by the func-
                            tional hamstring-to-quadriceps ratio, defined as the ratio between hamstring eccentric peak
                            torque (Hecc ) and quadriceps concentric peak torque (Qcon ). Other characteristics of these
                            athletes that might put them more at risk of ACLI include a low limb symmetry index
                            (LSI) [10], in particular in sports with very specific roles for each leg (kicking in football,
                            lunging in field hockey, for example), and the need for explosive force production and
                            quick changes in direction [12].
                                  Interestingly, the risk factors described above are also crucial factors to consider for
                            RTS after ACLI. Indeed, deficits in the strength developed by the quadriceps and ham-
                            strings are commonly reported in athletes, both at RTS and in the years following [13–16].
                            The hamstrings’ role as a synergist for the ACL is important in managing anterior tibial
                            translation during landing, with maximal strength deficits reported as a risk factor for
                            ACLI or re-injury in a number of prospective studies [17,18]. Quadriceps contractions help
                            to absorb GRF during performance, in turn attenuating loads on lower extremities, such as
                            the ACL during landing [19]. Deficits in quadriceps maximal strength have been associated
                            with the incidence of re-injury following ACLI [20]. For both these muscle groups, it is
                            commonly accepted that an LSI greater than 90% between operated and non-operated legs
                            should be sufficient to reduce the risk of future damage to the surgical graft [20]. Despite
                            this stipulation, many athletes still RTS with strength deficits in both muscle groups at RTS
                            and in the years following, making appropriate rehabilitation essential [13,15,16].
                                  More recently, authors have investigated quadriceps and hamstring force produced
                            close to knee extension as risk factors because ACLI seem to occur at these angles [21,22],
                            while peak values occur mid-range [23]. Hammond [24] identified that within a cohort of
                            previously injured athletes who met initial criteria of LSI > 90% for maximal strength of
                            the quadriceps and hamstrings, strength deficiencies were still observed in 72% of them, in
                            particular at 10- 40◦ from full extension.
                                  As mentioned earlier, the capacity to quickly produce force (rate of force or torque
                            development, RFD or RTD) is a strong predictor of ACLI, in particular for the hamstring [24].
                            Indeed, most ACLI occurs within 0–61ms of initial contact with the ground [25]. The use of
                            RFD, despite its relevance, remains very limited for RTS testing following ACLR [26], yet
                            deficits in RFD are commonly seen following ACLR [27,28].
                                  To our knowledge, only one study has examined the relationship between strength
                            performance and psychological variables following ACLR utilising the anterior cruciate lig-
                            ament return to sport after injury (ACL-RSI) questionnaire to quantify patient psychological
                            readiness to RTS [29]. This study showed a significant association between ACL-RSI scores
                            and hamstring peak torque, but not quadriceps, in a cohort of male athletes at 9 months
                            post-surgery [29]. Additional findings from this study were the absence of significant
                            differences in peak strength variables between a group with a low ACL-RSI score (<65)
                            and a group with a high ACL-RSI score (>85). However, this study only measured peak
                            strength, and there are currently no investigations on the association between ACL-RSI
                            scores and other strength parameters, such as RFD or angle-specific torque.
                                  Therefore, the primary aim of the present study was to investigate the strength and
                            power determinants of athletes’ psychological readiness to RTS. A secondary aim was
                            to compare strength and power performance of a group deemed psychologically ready
                            for a return to PILOS against those deemed not psychologically ready to return to PILOS.
                            We hypothesised that the group deemed not psychologically ready for a return to PILOS

                            psychologically ready to return to PILOS.

                            2. Materials and Methods
                            2.1. Participants
                                 Twelve participants, including six males and six females (20.7 ± 2.5 years old;
                            174.2 ± 7.5 cm; 70.2 ± 8.5 kg; 18.2 ± 8.3% body fat) volunteered to take part in the study.
                            They were recruited from various university teams competing at regional to national levels.
                            Inclusion criteria were having a primary ACLR more than 9 months prior to the start of the
                            study because most athletes are cleared for RTS support between 6–9-month post-surgery.
                            To be included in the study participants should also have already returned to some form of
                            sport participation or have been officially cleared to do so by a qualified physiotherapist.
                            Exclusion criteria were any current lower limb injury, any history of contralateral ACLI or
                            recurrent ipsilateral ACLR, and any mental health condition, such as depression or anxiety,
                            that could influence ACLI-RSI scores [30]. Participants gave written informed consent
                            and the study was approved by the local university ethics committee (reference number
                            191305), in accordance with the principles set in the Helsinki declaration.

                            2.2. Procedures
                                  The study design was cross-sectional, with participants attending the laboratory on
                            one occasion only to perform psychological assessments first, followed by strength testing.
                            The same investigator performed all the tests on all participants.
                                  Psychological assessment consisted of the ACL-RSI questionnaire. This questionnaire
                            was chosen for its very good validity and reliability [31,32]. In addition, its use was
                            recommended in the 2015 consensus statement following ACLI [3]. The total score out of
                            100 was recorded, and it was also used to separate participants into one group deemed
                            not psychologically ready to return to PILOS (cases) and a group deemed psychologically
                            ready to return to PILOS (controls). The threshold used for these groups was a total score of
                            81.4%, as a previous study reported an association between scores <81.4% and the inability
                            for athletes to return to this level [31].
                                  Strength testing was undertaken on an isokinetic dynamometer (Biodex system 4;
                            Biodex, Shirley, NY, USA). A standardised warm up was implemented prior to the initiation
                            of isokinetic testing. This consisted of 8 min on a Monark cycle ergometer (874E; Monark,
                            Vanberg, Sweden) at an intensity of 100 W, with three intermittent 6 s maximal effort sprints
                            at minutes 6, 7, and 8. This was followed by five body-weight squats and two submaximal
                            and three maximal counter-movement jumps [29]. After the warm-up, participants were
                            instructed to sit upright on the chair with their hips flexed at 90◦ . Straps were secured
                            to immobilise movement at the thighs, hips, and trunk in order to limit the influence
                            of extraneous joint and muscle involvement. Straps were secured at the proximal tibias,
                            from which participants would initiate/resist movement. Alignment of the lateral femoral
                            condyle was made with the axis of the dynamometer level arm, with the proximal lever
                            arm secured at the lateral malleolus. Participants were tested on both operated and non-
                            operated legs and at two angular velocities, with all of these conditions randomised. The
                            range of motion was from 0◦ (full knee extension) to 90◦ of knee flexion, and participants
                            were given verbal encouragement to perform the fastest and strongest contraction effort
                            throughout the range. The test consisted of concentric contractions of the quadriceps and
                            eccentric contraction of the hamstrings at 60◦ ·s−1 (three repetitions) and 180◦ ·s−1 (five
                            repetitions). Five repetitions have been recommended in previous studies at 180◦ ·s−1
                            because it takes more repetitions to reach peak torque and it also induces less fatigue than
                            slower velocities [24]. These velocities are characterised by excellent test–retest reliability
                            (intraclass correlation coefficients of 0.95–0.98 [33]. Each condition was preceded by a
                            familiarisation set.
                                  The following variables were calculated as the average of the two best contractions at
                            60◦ ·s−1 and the three best contractions at 180◦ ·s−1 :

                            2.3. Statistical Analyses
                                  All data were presented as mean ± standard deviation, with a 95% confidence interval
                            (CI). Statistical analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS V.29. The normality of data was
                            assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test. A stepwise linear regression was conducted on the
                            entire sample to identify if strength data from the operated leg could be determinants
                            of the ACL-RSI score. Subsequently, participants were divided into a ready to return to
                            PILOS group and not ready to return to PILOS group. A mixed model analysis of variance
                            (ANOVA) with repeated measures was performed to assess differences between groups
                            (ready vs. not ready to return to PILOS) and angular velocities (60◦ ·s−1 vs. 180◦ ·s−1 )
                            on all outcome variables. Effect sizes were calculated as partial eta squared (η2 p ) for the
                            ANOVA and interpreted as no effect (0–0.05), minimum effect (0.05–0.26), and strong effect
                            (0.26–0.64), while Cohen’s d (d) represented the effect size for post-hoc tests, and were
                            interpreted as small (>0.2), medium (>0.5), and large (>0.8), [38]. The p-value was set at
                            p < 0.05.

                            3. Results
                                  We recruited participants from football (n = 4), volleyball (n = 2), netball (n = 2),
                            lacrosse (n = 2), tennis (n = 1), and triathlon (n = 1). Seven participants were identified as
                            cases with ACL-RSI scores <81.4% and five participants were identified as controls with
                            ACL-RSI scores > 81.5. Participant Demographics are summarised in Table 1.
                                  The linear regression identified that three variables, namely quadriceps RTD100 at
                            60◦ ·s−1 , time since surgery, and hamstrings RTD50 at 60◦ ·s−1 , were significant predictors of
                            the ACL-RSI score (r2 = 0.915). The statistics associated with each factor were beta = 0.583,
                            t = 5.077 (p < 0.001) for quadriceps RTD100 at 60◦ ·s−1 ; beta = 0.620, t = 5.855 (p < 0.001) for
                            time since surgery; and beta = 0.411, t = 3.498 (p = 0.008) for hamstrings RTD50 at 60◦ ·s−1 .

                            4. Discussion
                                 This study is one of very few observing the relationship between strength and power
                            parameters and psychological readiness following ACLR. We measured a range of param-
                            eters during concentric contractions of the quadriceps and eccentric contractions of the
                            hamstrings, since these antagonist muscles are involved in many sport movements. In
                            particular, the hamstrings act as an ACL agonist by eccentrically contracting to decelerate
                            the anterior translation of the tibia during powerful quadriceps contractions. The main
                            findings are that the RTD of the quadriceps and hamstrings, as well as time since surgery,
                            were the main determinants of psychological readiness following ACLR. In addition, com-
                            pared to controls, cases showed significantly lower angle-specific Qcon close to extension
                            and lower RTD for Qcon , but no difference in peak torque values.
                                 We recruited athletes mostly from team contact sports, despite advertising the study
                            to all university sports. It is not very surprising due to the high occurrence of ACLI
                            reported in these sports [9]. It is well established that athletes from these sports show
                            similar neuromuscular characteristics that could make them more at risk of ACLI, such as
                            low Hecc :Qcon or high LSI [10,11].
                                 A novel finding identified within this study is the extent to which RTD has been
                            identified as both a determinant for psychological readiness and as a statistically significant
                            difference between groups. This is the first study to examine the relationships between
                            muscle RTD scores and psychological readiness, and, therefore, a comparison of results
                            cannot be made against previous literature. The prevalence of RFD as a power deficit
                            following ACLR, however, is well reported for the injured limb in the short term [27,28] but
                            also in the longer term [39]. Deficits in RFD following ACLR could be due to both neural
                            and peripheral muscular factors [39,40] and seem to closely reflect athletes’ rehabilitation
                            status [39]. Several training modalities can improve RFD; for example, ballistic training
                            performed around RTS [41] has shown greater increases in RFD than traditional strength
                            and endurance training [42]. Sprint training also increased RFD (+29% in four weeks)
                            in a recent study, while strength training did not [43]. With a potential overreliance on
                            isolated maximal muscle strength after ACLR within traditional RTS training [41], results
                            from this study indicate a greater focus should be given to training methods including a
                            speed/power element in the facilitation of a successful RTS. Examples of such exercises
                            include jump squats, mountain climbers, plank jacks, and skater hops for quadriceps power
                            gain, and hurdle jumps, box jumps, jumping lunges, and resisted sprinting for hamstrings
                            power gain. Physiotherapists should also monitor RTD (or RFD) during rehabilitation and
                            consider it as an important variable for RTS. To explain the impact of RTD on psychological
                            outcomes shown in the present study, the functional role played by the hamstrings and
                            quadriceps in providing stability at the knee needs to be considered [44,45]. The ability
                            of muscles to generate force within an early critical window (0–100 ms) is essential for
                            stabilising the leg, attenuating GRF [19], and aligning landing mechanics within the period
                            of time in which ACLI occur [25]. With residual movement impairments during RTS, it
                            may be theorised that such neuromuscular deficits will affect the quality of movement
                            athletes display [41], which may be negatively perceived by athletes, subsequently altering
                            their ACL-RSI scores. These assumptions rely on the biopsychosocial framework, where an
                            athlete’s physiological factors have a mediating role in their psychological perceptions [3].
                            However, further experimental studies should be conducted to confirm these associations.
                                 The role of peak torque as a determinant of ACL-RSI scores was not identified in the
                            present study, suggesting that maximal force production might not be as important as
                            sport staff (coaches, physiotherapists, and strength and conditioning staff) or researchers
                            thought. This is partly in line with the findings of the only study in this area reporting no
                            significant relationship between peak Qcon at 60◦ ·s−1 and ACL-RSI scores in athletes nine
                            months post-surgery [29]. However, the same authors also showed a small but significant
                            correlation (r = 0.14) between peak Hecc at 60◦ ·s−1 and ACL-RSI scores [29], which is in
                            contrast with our results. The study of O’Connor et al. [29] also separated participants
                            according to their ACL-RSI scores, similar to the present study, and found no significant
 Healthcare 2023, 11, 2787                                                                                            9 of 12




                            between-group differences in peak Qcon or peak Hecc , in accordance with our results. The
                            contrasting results on Hecc between the present study and the study of O’Connor et al. [29]
                            could be explained by the different criteria used to separate groups (low (<65) and high
                            (>85) ACL-RSI scores for cases and controls in the study by O’Connor et al. [29] compared
                            to <81.4% and >81.4% in the present study). Having some individuals from different groups
                            but with very close ACL-RSI scores in the present study could have biassed the results
                            towards a lack of between-group differences. Other differences between studies are the
                            significantly larger sample size in O’Connor [29]’s study (n = 452) and their cut-off at nine
                            months post-surgery, compared to the range of longitudinal time frames examined within
                            this study. It can be hypothesised that athlete perceptions within O’Connor’s [29] study
                            are more of a reflection of their rehabilitation process. In contrast, for our participants who
                            have returned to sport and, thus, benefit from greater sporting exposures, ACL-RSI scores
                            illustrate the development of psychological barriers for athletes in the pursuit of a return to
                            PILOS, which is a novel element of the current study. Finally, our data analysis was based
                            on a linear regression, in contrast to correlations in the study of O’Connor et al. [29], which
                            may explain the lack of association between some parameters and the ACL-RSI scores.
                                  A novel finding of the present study is the significantly lower Qcon40 and Qcon30 in
                            cases compared to controls (differences of 21% and 23%, respectively, at these angles). The
                            role of the quadriceps at these shallow flexion angles is significant in relation to the number
                            of ACLI that occur within them [21]. Previous studies have shown that individuals with
                            weaker quadriceps have altered sagittal plane kinematics during landing and subsequently
                            incur higher GRF upon a stiff-legged landing [19]. Similar to our comments on RTD, this
                            process may result in a perception of instability during sport participation that could be
                            reflected in the ACL-RSI scores. During rehabilitation, restoration of joint ROM is targeted
                            during the early phases [46], yet little consideration is noted regarding muscular strength,
                            specifically functionally important ranges (near full knee extension) in which non-contact
                            ACLI occur (Hammond [24]). Our findings on angle-specific torque, together with the
                            absence of significant differences between groups in peak torque, highlight the importance
                            for physiotherapists to address strength deficits across the full range of motion and consider
                            sport-specific mechanics (i.e., movements such as landing or side cutting, where the knee
                            might not be very flexed, supporting stipulations made by Hammond [24], who similarly
                            reported strength deficits between specific angles, where >90% LSI was achieved during
                            peak torque assessments). The importance of the capacity to produce high torque when
                            the knee is close to full extension has also been highlighted in a study on fatigue in female
                            footballers, showing that Hecc :Qcon was significantly reduced after a simulated match only
                            between 0 and 10◦ from full knee extension [34]. This highlights the reduced capacity
                            of the hamstring to stabilise the knee joint close to extension in a fatigued state, where
                            ACLI occurs, and highlights the importance of addressing residual strength deficits at these
                            angles during rehabilitation.
                                  The limb symmetry index has been cited as a risk factor for lower limb injuries in
                            previous literature [47], although there are contrasting results in the literature [48]. Our
                            findings did not identify it as a major determinant of psychological readiness to RTS,
                            suggesting that it might not be sensitive enough to affect athletes’ perceptions during
                            exercise. However, we found that LSI for RTD100 in the quadriceps at both testing velocities
                            was greater in cases than controls. This highlights one more time that power rather than
                            strength could be an important factor that could play a role in athletes’ decisions to RTS.
                                  The main limitations of the present study are the lack of control over our participants’
                            rehabilitation and subsequent sport experience. Indeed, we could not capture the exercise
                            types, volume, and frequency of rehabilitation sessions or past/current sport participation
                            due to the long time lapse between the start of rehabilitation and testing for some of our
                            participants. In addition, we chose to focus on psychological parameters as our main
                            outcome and explore the role of strength and power variables as potential determinants
                            of this. However, an argument can be made that constructs such as fear and confidence
                            may instead impact physiological parameters through the avoidance of high-intensity
 Healthcare 2023, 11, 2787                                                                                                           10 of 12




                                   rehabilitation required in order to efficiently address them. Finally, our sample size was
                                   small, in particular in comparison with the study by O’Connor et al. [29], which could
                                   limit the interpretation of our findings; however, this is counteracted by the fact that we
                                   observed relatively large effect sizes. We also recruited athletes from specific sports, which
                                   might limit the application of our findings to other sports. The main strengths of our
                                   study are the wide and novel range of outcome variables considered (in particular, RTD
                                   and angle-specific torque data) and the controlled laboratory conditions in which data
                                   was collected.

                                   5. Conclusions
                                         In conclusion, our findings showed that one of the main determinants of psychological
                                   readiness to RTS following ACLR was the RTD of the quadriceps and hamstrings. In
                                   addition, compared to controls, cases showed significantly lower angle-specific quadriceps
                                   torque close to extension and lower quadriceps RTD, but no difference in peak torque values.
                                   The importance of muscular strength across all angles of function was also identified, with
                                   quadriceps strength of particular importance at angles of functional relevance between 20◦
                                   and 40◦ from full extension. These findings highlight the importance for physiotherapists
                                   to address muscular deficits across their full range (by choosing some exercises with the
                                   knee joint positioned near full extension) and develop power and explosiveness in addition
                                   to strength in rehabilitation. Future studies with larger sample sizes are needed to further
                                   investigate the relationship between strength and power and psychological factors playing
                                   a role in RTS.

                                   Author Contributions: O.T.L. conducted the data collection, statistical analysis and write-up. A.D.
                                   designed the study and supervised statistical analysis and write-up. M.A.W. designed the study and
                                   helped with the write-up. C.D.S. helped with the write-up and analysis. All authors have read and
                                   agreed to the published version of the manuscript.

                                   Institutional Review Board Statement: The study was approved by the local university ethics
                                   committee (reference number 191305).
                                   Informed Consent Statement: Informed consent was obtained from all subjects involved in the study.

  "abstract": "The review summarizes virtual reality (VR) approaches for football injuries, covering prevention (biomechanical risk assessment, perceptual-cognitive training, heading), rehabilitation (low back pain, return to sport, kinesiophobia) and concussion education.   "findings": "The review's tables list 14 studies, mostly single-session laboratory work with 2 to 60 participants. Reported results include VR training improving passing decisions and visual search in young players (Fortes et al., 2021), VR-trained players scoring more headed goals than controls over 10 days (Marshall et al., 2023), and VR reducing pain and kinesiophobia in players with chronic low back pain (Nambi et al.). A single-session VR concussion education study in children (Sullivan et al., 2024) found no significant change in attitudes toward reporting or reporting intentions.",
  "limitations": "The authors state that there is no standardized VR protocol and no randomized controlled trial of VR exercise efficacy, and that the reliability of VR movement analysis in sport is unproven.   "practicalImplications": "Sports medicine and performance staff may consider VR as a supplement for perceptual-cognitive or biomechanical training and for low back pain or fear-of-movement work, where the evidence is preliminary.   "athleteDev": "VR is a possible training aid for decision-making and heading skills in footballers, based on small studies with short follow-up. Coaches should not expect large or proven performance gains from it.",

}

74	                                Muscle strains, ligament sprains and contusions were the most common, with thigh
75	                          strain representing 17% of all injuries, and posterior thigh strains more common than
76	                          anterior ones. Furthermore, adductor pain/strain, ankle sprain and medial collateral
77	                          ligament (MCL) injuries are relatively frequent [3].
78	                                Muscle injuries constitute 31% of all injuries and cause 27% of total injury absences. In
79	                          total, 92% of all muscle injuries affect the four major lower limb muscle groups: hamstrings
80	                          (37%), adductors (23%), quadriceps (19%), and calf muscles (13%). Moreover, quadriceps
81	                          strains (60%) affect mostly the dominant leg (preferred kicking leg) and the incidence
82	                          is six times higher during a match compared with training [3,4]. Muscle injuries have
83	                          been classified into non-structural and structural injuries [5]: non-structural lesions, which
84	                          comprise 70% of muscle injuries in football, do not lead to theanatomical interruption of
85	                          muscle fibers. In these cases, the athlete usually reports tenderness, heaviness, or a feeling
86	                          of stiffness in the affected muscle, which increases with the continuation of sports activity
87	                          and sometimes occurs at rest. Upon palpatory examination, stiffer muscle bundles can be
88	                          found within the interested muscle. Moreover, re-injury represents a serious concern by
89	                          causing more prolonged absences, and players with a history of previous injuries tend to
90	                          have a re-injury risk that is 4 to 7 times greater [3].
91	                                What predisposes the athlete to a relapse is both risk factors related to the changes that
92	                          occurred after the first injury (muscle hypotrophy, scar tissue, neuromuscular changes), as
93	                          well as inadequate treatments (aggressive or incomplete rehabilitation, underestimation of
94	                          primary injury, prolonged immobilization).
95	                                In addition to muscle injuries, one of the most common injuries concerns ligaments;
96	                          in particular, anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture has a serious impact on footballers’
97	                          careers. The ACL provides stability to the knee joint, preventing the anterior displacement
98	                          of the tibia relative to the femur. A complete rupture is a cause of knee instability and can
99	                          lead to long-term knee conditions, such as meniscosis, osteoarthritis, and a high rate of new
100	                          lesions in the graft or contralateral knee [6,7]. A study based on 78 teams participating in
101	                          UEFA competitions between 2001 and 2015 recorded 157 cruciate ligament injuries, of which
102	                          140 were total and 17 were partial ruptures, including six relapses and two contralateral
103	                          injuries; the average frequency of cruciate ligament injuries is 0.066 per 1000 h. The full
104	                          injury had a significantly higher average frequency than partial rupture (0.059 vs. 0.007 per
105	                          1000 h), and the frequency of injuries during matches was greater than 20 times compared
106	                          to workout [8]. ACL injuries usually occur through traumatic mechanisms without contact,
107	                          mainly during high-velocity movements, such as a quick change of direction, a sudden
108	                          stop, or a landing after a jump [8].
109	                                One of the most discussed risk factors for injuries is fatigue, defined not as energy
110	                          exhaustion during a game, but an effect of fatigue accumulation over a period of time,
111	                          presumably due to a dense schedule of matches [9]. In addition, several intrinsic and
112	                          extrinsic factors pose a higher risk of injuries, such as intrinsic biomechanical factors,
113	                          hormonal, anatomical and neuromuscular risk factors, as well as limited hip and ankle
114	                          mobility, which could predispose the knee to higher loads [10]. There are also some gender-
115	                          related risk factors, which show that female populations have a particular predisposition
116	                          (e.g., for ACL injuries), presumably due to the role of estrogen receptors and progesterone
117	                          in female populations [11].
118	                                Injuries are therefore a serious problem not only for players but also for clubs as, on
119	                          the one hand, the chances of the whole team performing optimally are limited; on the other
120	                          hand, they also represent a cost to society (the average cost of a professional player injured
121	                          for a month is about EUR 500.000) [8].

123	                          1.2. Injury Prevention
124	                               Injury prevention is essential for reducing the long-term consequences and minimizing
125	                          the impact on the sports season. It is recommended that an approach be based on the

130	                          individual athlete’s lifestyle, not solely on managing risk factors. Several injury prevention
131	                          programs like FIFA 11+ and PEP have been developed in recent years [12,13].
132	                                The focus is the perception of the fatigue of athletes, which can be avoided by main-
133	                          taining proper hydration, nutrition, and following individualized training protocols with
134	                          appropriate loads. Moreover, muscle weakness and the difference in strength between
135	                          agonist and antagonist muscles increase the risk of injury by 4 to 5 times. Therefore, it is
136	                          crucial to objectively and quantitatively evaluate athletes periodically [14,15].
137	                                Prevention exercise programs with a comprehensive approach play a key role in
138	                          reducing the incidence of injury. It has been shown that specific prevention programs such
139	                          as Sportsmetrics and the Prevent Injury and Enhance Performance Program reduce the risk
140	                          of injury and positively impact performances [16].
141	                                Eccentric exercise training is the method most used for preventive purposes because it
142	                          causes a muscle adaptation that significantly improves the stiffness of the muscle–tendon
143	                          unit. Moreover, proprioceptive training has also shown interesting results; it must be
144	                          preceded by adequate heating, in monopodalic and bipodalic alternating support, on stable
145	                          and unstable surfaces with dynamic exercises and adequate technical material [17]. Finally,
146	                          selective core muscle training can also improve the neuromuscular control of the lower
147	                          limbs, and working on balance has been proven effective in reducing the rate of anterior
148	                          cruciate ligament injuries [10].
149	
150	                          1.3. Rehabilitation
151	                                In case of injury, rehabilitation is of vital importance, with specific treatments based
152	                          on the type and site of injury, and the grade of lesion. In most injuries, the treatment is
153	                          conservative, with reduced workloads, active recovery with hydrokinesitherapy and the
154	                          application of physical therapies [7]. The type of rehabilitation and therapeutic proposals
155	                          must respect the principle of specificity, progression, and individualization. It is essential to
156	                          consider pain as an indicative factor for the load capacity, with a progressive load needed
157	                          to allow complete and optimal tissue regeneration [18,19]. When returning to play, it is
158	                          important to apply the correct progression of sport-specific training, which is enabled
159	                          by the sanitary staff’s constant monitoring and correct communication with the technical
160	                          staff [6].
161	                                In case of surgical treatment, pre-operative rehabilitation is fundamental, with the aim
162	                          to control pain and inflammation through cryotherapy, compression and anti-inflammatory
163	                          drugs, the recovery of ROM through active and passive mobilizations, and the strengthen-
164	                          ing of quadriceps and hamstrings through exercises in the closed kinetic chain, possibly by
165	                          using electrical stimulation and proprioceptive education [20].
166	
167	                          1.4. Virtual Reality
168	                                Alongside the classic rehabilitation techniques and various protocols for injury man-
169	                          agement, we have observed the swift advancement of new technologies such as virtual
170	                          reality (VR). VR can be defined as “a medium comprising interactive computer simulations
171	                          that detect the position and movements of the subject, giving the feeling of being mentally
172	                          immersed in the virtual world”.
173	                                Through various tools, including headsets, gloves, shoes and joypads, the experience
174	                          is enriched, and the three-dimensional environment appears real [21].
175	                                It is possible to distinguish three types of virtual reality, each with its specific charac-
176	                          teristics [21,22]:
177	                          •    Immersive VR creates a three-dimensional room in which the subject is immersed with
178	                               no reference to the real world.
179	                          •    Non-immersive VR is generated through computers and consoles, allowing the visual-
180	                               ization of 2D virtual objects in the real context.
181	                          •    Mixed reality combines immersive and non-immersive virtual reality: the technology
182	                               is generated by head-mounted displays that overlap with the real-world 3D virtual
183	                               objects (holograms), allowing interaction with them.

188	                                In the medical field, VR has shown interesting results in numerous applications,
189	                          mainly in motor and cognitive rehabilitation and the therapy of psychiatric disorders, such
190	                          as anxiety and depression [23]. Currently, VR-based rehabilitation is used particularly in
191	                          the neurological field for balance disorders and impairment of the upper limbs following
192	                          stroke [22].
193	                                This technology has become increasingly popular in recent years, as it provides a
194	                          secure and controlled environment for performing various actions. In addition, using VR
195	                          constitutes a motivating and engaging rehabilitation approach for the patient, with the
196	                          possibility to customize the treatment based on the patient’s needs [9].
197	                                Among the critical issues that emerge from the use of VR in healthcare are the costs of
198	                          equipment, the need for technical expertise, and cybersickness, defined as the nausea and
199	                          headaches caused by the prolonged use of smartphones, tablets and headsets [24].
200	                                In sport, VR can be seen as an assistive technology that provides specific support
201	                          for training through the simulation of game dynamics and data analysis. However, the
202	                          applications of VR vary, and include the improvement of teamwork and reductions in the
203	                          risk of injury throughout a personalized training program for a single player based on the
204	                          data collected, helping them to improve their weaknesses and reach their potential [24,25].
205	                                In addition, athletes who undergo a rehabilitation program involving VR describe the
206	                          experience as rewarding, pleasant and motivating, increasing their compliance [26].
207	                                VR’s interactive and immersive nature can aid in conducting training sessions and
208	                          enable accurate statistical analysis. Athletes can practice on a simulated field using headsets
209	                          and head-mounted displays while collecting and analyzing crucial data in real time, e.g.,
210	                          heart rate and blood pressure, to evaluate the effectiveness of their training [24].
211	                                To the best of our knowledge, no previous study has summarized the role of VR in
212	                          the management of football injuries. Thus, the aim of this narrative review is to provide
213	                          a broad overview of the currently available VR approaches used to reduce the incidence
214	                          of injuries and improve the rehabilitation outcome, promoting a personalized strategy for
215	                          the multidisciplinary management of footballers. In details, this review analyzes the role
216	                          of VR for preventive purposes through a study of the biomechanics of athletic gestures
217	                          in a realistic environment and the reduction in concussions; the rehabilitative purposes,
218	                          improvements in pain symptoms, return to sport, and kinesiophobia are also analyzed.
